11.  
Governments use fiscal policy—changes in government spending and taxation—to influence aggregate demand (AD) and stabilize the economy over the business cycle.

- During a recession (negative output gap, high unemployment), governments typically pursue expansionary fiscal policy:  
  - Increase government spending (G) on goods, services, and transfers  
  - Decrease taxes (T) to raise disposable income and consumption  
  This shifts AD to the right, increasing output and employment.

- During an expansion or boom (positive output gap, inflationary pressure), governments may use contractionary fiscal policy:  
  - Decrease G  
  - Increase T  
  This shifts AD to the left, cooling inflationary pressures.

Automatic stabilizers—like progressive income taxes and unemployment benefits—also help: tax revenues fall and transfers rise in recessions (supporting AD) and the opposite occurs in expansions (restraining AD) without new legislation each time. Discretionary fiscal measures (deliberate policy changes) can reinforce or supplement these automatic effects when downturns or booms are large.

12.  
Inflation can arise from two main sources: demand-pull and cost-push forces.

- Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand grows faster than aggregate supply at or near full employment. Causes include:  
  - Expansionary monetary policy (low interest rates, increased money supply)  
  - Expansionary fiscal policy (higher G, lower T)  
  - Increases in private consumption, investment, or net exports  
  When AD persistently exceeds the economy’s capacity, prices are bid up.

- Cost-push inflation originates on the supply side, when firms’ production costs rise and are passed on as higher prices even if demand is unchanged. Causes include:  
  - Rising wages not matched by productivity gains (wage-push)  
  - Increases in prices of key inputs (e.g., oil, commodities, imported inputs)  
  - Higher indirect taxes or regulatory costs  
  These shift short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) left, raising the price level and often reducing output (stagflation).

In practice, inflation dynamics often involve both: excess demand can tighten labor markets and push up wages, while adverse supply shocks (like energy price spikes) can trigger cost-push inflation that monetary and fiscal authorities must then manage.

  - Expansionary fiscal policy (higher G, lower T)  
  - Increases in private consumption, investment, or net exports  
  When AD persistently exceeds the economy’s capacity, prices are bid up.

- Cost-push inflation originates on the supply side, when firms’ production costs rise and are passed on as higher prices even if demand is unchanged. Causes include:  
  - Rising wages not matched by productivity gains (wage-push)  
  - Increases in prices of key inputs (e.g., oil, commodities, imported inputs)  
  - Higher indirect taxes or regulatory costs  
  These shift short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) left, raising the price level and often reducing output (stagflation).

In practice, inflation dynamics often involve both: excess demand can tighten labor markets and push up wages, while adverse supply shocks (like energy price spikes) can trigger cost-push inflation that monetary and fiscal authorities must then manage.
